title: Parmenides and Zeno: Being and Paradox
subtitle: Two philosophers from Elea who argued that change is impossible, and dared you to prove them wrong
objectives: Describe Parmenides’ poem and the difference between the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion
Reconstruct Parmenides’ argument that what-is cannot come into being, perish or change
Explain three of Zeno’s paradoxes of motion (the Dichotomy, Achilles and the Arrow) and how they work as arguments
Evaluate the main responses to Zeno, from Aristotle to modern mathematics
Explain why the conflict between reason and the senses became a central problem for later philosophy
hook:
Try a simple experiment. Walk toward a door. Before you can reach it, you must first get halfway there. Before you finish the remaining distance, you must get halfway through that. Then halfway through what is left, and so on. There will always be another half to cross, an endless series of smaller and smaller journeys. How, then, does anyone ever reach the door?

You know perfectly well that you will reach the door. Your eyes and legs tell you so. But can you say exactly what is wrong with the argument? For more than two thousand years, some very clever people could not agree on an answer. The argument comes from Zeno of Elea, who invented it to defend his teacher Parmenides, a philosopher who claimed something far stranger: that change, motion and even the existence of many separate things are illusions. Yesterday Heraclitus told us that everything flows. Today two men from a small town in southern Italy reply that nothing does.

sections.heading: A Journey to the Goddess
sections.body:
**Parmenides** came from Elea, a Greek colony on the west coast of southern Italy, south of modern Naples. His dates are uncertain. Plato, in his dialogue *Parmenides*, describes him visiting Athens at about the age of 65, accompanied by Zeno, and talking with a very young Socrates. If that meeting happened, it was around 450 BCE, which would put Parmenides’ birth around 515 BCE. Plato may have invented the conversation, but the dating is widely used. Parmenides was apparently also respected in Elea as a lawgiver.

Unlike Heraclitus, who wrote in riddling prose, Parmenides wrote a **poem** in the same verse form as Homer’s epics. About 160 lines survive, mostly because a 6th-century CE commentator named Simplicius copied out long passages, saying the book had become rare.

The poem opens with a dramatic scene. A young man is carried in a chariot by the daughters of the Sun, along a road toward the gates of Night and Day. The goddess Justice holds the keys; the daughters persuade her to open them; and beyond, an unnamed goddess welcomes the traveler. She promises to teach him two things: the unshaken heart of well-rounded truth, and the opinions of mortals, in which there is no true reliability.

This is a strange way to begin a work of logic. Some scholars see the journey as an allegory of moving from ignorance to enlightenment; others think Parmenides was presenting a genuine religious revelation, perhaps connected to the healing and dream cults of southern Italy. But notice what the goddess actually does once the journey is over. She does not simply announce truths. She argues. She tells the young man to judge her claims by reason, by *logos*. The setting is mythical, but the content is a chain of reasoning, and that is what made Parmenides revolutionary.

sections.heading: The Way of Truth: What Is, Is
sections.body:
The goddess says there are only two conceivable paths of inquiry. One is that it is, and it cannot not be. The other is that it is not, and it must not be. The second, she says, is a path that cannot be learned at all, because you could not know what is not, nor point it out (Fragment B2). And she adds a line that is one of the most discussed in philosophy: for the same thing is there for thinking and for being (B3). In other words, whatever can be thought or spoken of must exist. **Nothing**, strictly speaking, cannot be thought.

Scholars argue about what the subject of “it is” is. Being in general? Whatever can be investigated? Reality as a whole? The poem never says. Most beginners can follow it best by reading it as **what-is**, or **Being**: whatever is real.

Now comes the crucial move. Once we agree that what-is-not cannot be thought or spoken of, a great deal follows. In Fragment B8, the goddess lists the signs along the true road, and argues for each. What-is must be:

- **Ungenerated and imperishable.** Could what-is have come into being? From what? Not from what-is-not, because there is no such thing. Not from what-is, because then it already existed. Besides, she asks, what need would have driven it to start later rather than earlier? Similarly, it cannot perish into nothing.
- **Whole and indivisible.** It cannot be more here and less there, because there is nothing other than what-is to separate one part from another. It is all continuous.
- **Unchanging and motionless.** Change means something becoming what it was not. But that requires the forbidden notion of not-being.
- **Complete.** It lacks nothing, and the goddess compares it to the mass of a well-rounded sphere, equally balanced in every direction.

She even says it never was, nor will be, since it is now, all together. Past and future seem to require what-is-no-longer and what-is-not-yet, so they too are ruled out.

The conclusion is breathtaking. Reality is one, eternal, undivided and changeless. The view that reality is ultimately a single thing is called **monism**. The world of many separate things, born, growing, moving and dying, which our senses show us every moment, is not the truth.

sections.heading: Reason Against the Senses
sections.body:
What should we do when our senses and our reasoning disagree? Parmenides had a clear answer. The goddess warns the young man not to let habit force him to wander along the road of experience, using an aimless eye and an echoing ear and tongue. Instead he must judge by reason (B7). She also mocks ordinary mortals as two-headed and helpless, people who think that to be and not to be are the same and not the same (B6). Many scholars hear a jab at Heraclitus in that line, though this is disputed.

This is the first clear statement in Western thought of a position that will run through the whole history of philosophy: that **reason**, not the senses, is the true guide to reality. Plato will take it up (Day 11), and so, much later, will the Rationalists such as Descartes. The opposite view, that knowledge must be built from experience, will be championed by Aristotle and later by the Empiricists. Parmenides set the terms of a debate that is still running.

But the poem has a surprising second half. After the Way of Truth, the goddess delivers what she calls the **Way of Opinion** (in Greek, *doxa*): an account of the cosmos as mortals see it, built from two opposing principles, light and night. It covers the heavens, the moon, the origin of living things. Parmenides seems to have done serious astronomy here; later writers credit him with knowing that the moon shines with light borrowed from the sun.

Why include a cosmology the goddess has just called unreliable? Scholars still disagree. Perhaps it shows the best account possible for those who trust the senses, so that the reader will not be fooled by worse ones. Perhaps it maps the mistakes of other thinkers. Perhaps Parmenides thought the world of appearances, though not ultimately real, still deserved careful description. The honest answer is that we do not know.

sections.heading: Zeno: Defending the Master With Paradox
sections.body:
Parmenides’ conclusions sounded absurd to many people, and they laughed at him. His younger fellow citizen **Zeno of Elea** (c. 490–c. 430 BCE) came to the rescue with a brilliant strategy. According to Plato’s *Parmenides*, Zeno explained that his book was a defense of Parmenides against those who mocked him. Zeno would not try to prove directly that reality is one and changeless. Instead he would show that the common-sense view, that there are many things and that they move, leads to consequences even more absurd.

This method is called **reductio ad absurdum** (Latin, “reduction to absurdity”): you assume your opponent’s claim, deduce something impossible from it, and conclude the claim must be false. A **paradox** is an argument that starts from apparently true assumptions, proceeds by apparently valid steps, and reaches an apparently false or contradictory conclusion. Something has to give. Aristotle later called Zeno the inventor of **dialectic**, the art of argument by question and refutation, which Socrates would make famous (Day 9).

Zeno reportedly wrote some forty arguments, mostly against plurality. The four most famous, against motion, survive mainly through Aristotle’s *Physics* (Book VI, chapter 9). Here are three.

1. **The Dichotomy.** To cross a distance, you must first cross half of it, then half of the rest, and so on forever. That is infinitely many tasks. No one can complete infinitely many tasks in a finite time. So no one can cross any distance, and motion is impossible. (A variant shows you could not even start, since before going half, you must go a quarter, and before that an eighth.)
2. **Achilles and the Tortoise.** Swift Achilles races a tortoise that has a head start. By the time Achilles reaches the point where the tortoise began, the tortoise has moved on a little. By the time he reaches that new point, it has moved on again. This repeats endlessly, so the fastest runner can never catch the slowest.
3. **The Arrow.** At any single instant, a flying arrow occupies a space exactly equal to itself. Something that occupies a space equal to itself at an instant is not moving at that instant. But the flight is made up entirely of instants. So the arrow is at rest throughout its flight.

The fourth, the Moving Rows (or Stadium), concerns bodies passing each other at different relative speeds, and its exact meaning is more disputed.

Zeno lived dramatically, according to legend. Several ancient sources say he plotted against a tyrant and, under torture, bit off his own tongue rather than betray his friends. The details vary from source to source, so treat it as legend. Parmenides’ cause also found another able defender in **Melissus** of Samos, who in 441 BCE commanded a fleet that defeated the Athenians. Melissus added a tidy argument: motion requires empty space to move into, but empty space would be what-is-not, which cannot exist. So nothing moves. Hold onto that argument. On Day 7 the atomists will turn it upside down.

sections.heading: Solving Zeno: An Unfinished Story
sections.body:
There is a story, told much later, that the Cynic philosopher Diogenes answered a lecture on the impossibility of motion by standing up and walking out. It is probably a legend, but it captures the obvious response: motion plainly exists. Yet that misses the point. Zeno knew people walk. His challenge was to show what is wrong with the reasoning. If you cannot, then your concepts of space, time and motion contain a hidden flaw.

**Aristotle** gave the first serious answer. He distinguished an actual infinity from a potential infinity. A distance is infinitely divisible in the sense that you *could* keep dividing it forever, but it is not actually composed of infinitely many pieces waiting to be crossed one by one. And the time it takes to cross the distance is divisible in exactly the same way, so infinitely many shrinking stretches of space are matched by infinitely many shrinking stretches of time. Against the Arrow, Aristotle denied that time is made of indivisible instants stacked together.

Modern mathematics offers another tool. In the 19th century, mathematicians including Augustin-Louis Cauchy and Karl Weierstrass gave rigorous definitions of a **limit** and of the sum of an infinite series. The series one half plus one quarter plus one eighth and so on, continued forever, has a finite sum: exactly 1. So infinitely many distances can add up to a finite distance, crossed in a finite time. Achilles catches the tortoise at a precise, calculable point. For the Arrow, mathematics now defines speed at an instant as a limit, not as movement during the instant. Bertrand Russell defended this so-called at-at theory: to move is simply to be at different places at different times, nothing more.

Many people think this settles the matter. Some philosophers disagree. Showing that an infinite series has a finite sum tells us what the total distance is, but does it explain how anyone actually *completes* an endless sequence of tasks, each of which comes after another with no last one? In 1954 the philosopher James Thomson sharpened this worry with an imaginary lamp switched on and off infinitely many times in two minutes. Is it on or off at the end? The worry about such supertasks shows that Zeno’s puzzles still provoke real debate.

Whatever their final solution, Parmenides and Zeno changed philosophy permanently. After them, no serious thinker could simply say that everything is made of water or air and turns into other things. They had to explain how change is possible at all without anything coming from nothing. The next three lessons are a series of answers to that challenge: the pluralists on Day 6, the atomists on Day 7, and, in a different way, Plato’s theory of Forms on Day 11.

keyQuote.text: For the same thing is there for thinking and for being.

modernConnection.title: The Block Universe and the Frames of a Film
modernConnection.body:
Parmenides sounds like the least modern thinker imaginable. Yet one of the most discussed pictures in contemporary physics has a distinctly Parmenidean feel. Einstein’s theory of relativity showed that whether two distant events happen at the same time depends on how the observer is moving. There is no single, universal “now” sweeping across the cosmos. Many physicists and philosophers conclude that past, present and future all exist equally, as parts of a four-dimensional spacetime. This picture is called the **block universe**, or eternalism. In it, nothing really “comes into being.” Your tenth birthday and your eightieth are simply different locations in the block, as real as different cities on a map. When his old friend Michele Besso died in 1955, Einstein wrote to Besso’s family that, for those who believe in physics, the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion.

Zeno’s Arrow also has a modern echo every time you watch a film or play a video game. A film is a series of still frames, usually 24 per second. In each frame nothing moves. Yet run them together and you see motion. Is real motion like that, a sequence of static states? Some speculative theories in physics even suggest that space and time might be granular at the tiniest scales, which would make Zeno’s endless halving impossible in the real world.

We should be honest about where the comparison breaks down. The block universe is not Parmenides’ One. It is rich with structure, containing billions of galaxies, while Parmenides’ Being has no parts at all. Physicists reach eternalism through experiment and mathematics, not by reflecting on the word “is.” And many physicists and philosophers reject the block universe, arguing that the flow of time is real. Still, the question Parmenides forced on us is alive: is change a basic feature of reality, or a feature of how limited creatures like us experience a reality that, seen whole, simply is?

vocabulary.definition: For Parmenides, whatever truly exists; he argued it must be eternal, one, undivided and unchanging.
vocabulary.example: Parmenides argued that Being cannot come from non-being, so it can never have begun.

vocabulary.definition: The first part of Parmenides’ poem, which argues by pure reason that what-is is ungenerated, indivisible and changeless.
vocabulary.example: In the Way of Truth, the goddess tells the traveler to judge by reason, not by the senses.

vocabulary.definition: The second part of Parmenides’ poem, a cosmology describing the world as it appears to mortals, which the goddess says lacks true reliability.
vocabulary.example: The Way of Opinion explains the heavens using two principles, light and night.

vocabulary.definition: The view that reality is ultimately one thing, or of one kind.
vocabulary.example: Parmenides’ monism is extreme: reality is a single, undivided whole.

vocabulary.definition: An argument that moves from apparently true premises, by apparently valid steps, to an apparently false or contradictory conclusion.
vocabulary.example: Achilles and the Tortoise is a paradox because each step seems fine but the conclusion is clearly false.

vocabulary.definition: A method of argument that assumes a claim, shows it leads to an absurd or contradictory result, and concludes that the claim is false.
vocabulary.example: Zeno used reductio ad absurdum, assuming motion exists in order to show that this leads to absurdity.

vocabulary.definition: The property of being divisible into smaller and smaller parts without end.
vocabulary.example: Zeno’s Dichotomy depends on the infinite divisibility of any distance.

vocabulary.definition: The art of reasoning through question, answer and refutation, testing a position by drawing out its consequences.
vocabulary.example: Aristotle named Zeno the inventor of dialectic, a method Socrates would make famous.

thinkingExercise.title: Find the Flaw
thinkingExercise.prompt: Zeno’s paradoxes are a workout for your reasoning. The goal is not to remember the official solution but to locate exactly where you think the argument goes wrong. Spend 10 to 15 minutes on paper.
steps: Write out the Dichotomy as a numbered list of premises and a conclusion, in your own words.
For each premise, mark whether you accept it, reject it or are unsure. Which premise would you give up, and why?
Take the Arrow. Do you think a moving object is “really” moving at a single instant? Write a short answer, then compare it with Russell’s at-at theory from the lesson.
Consider Parmenides’ claim that you cannot think of what-is-not. Try to think of “nothing.” What happens? Write two or three sentences on whether your experiment supports or undermines him.
Finally, note a case in your own life where reasoning told you one thing and your experience another. Which did you trust, and were you right?

summary: Parmenides of Elea (born c. 515 BCE) wrote a philosophical poem in which a goddess teaches the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion.
His core argument: what-is-not cannot be thought or exist, so what-is cannot come into being, perish, divide, move or change; reality is one, eternal and complete.
He insisted that reason, not the senses, is the judge of truth, launching a debate between reason and experience that runs through all of philosophy.
Zeno defended Parmenides with paradoxes (the Dichotomy, Achilles, the Arrow) designed to show that motion and plurality lead to absurdity, using reductio ad absurdum.

Aristotle answered with the distinction between potential and actual infinity; modern mathematics uses limits and convergent series, though some philosophers think puzzles about completing infinitely many tasks remain.
After the Eleatics, every philosopher had to explain how change is possible without anything coming from nothing, which sets the agenda for Days 6 and 7.

quiz.question: In what form did Parmenides write his philosophy?
options: A collection of riddling prose sayings
A dialogue between Socrates and his students
A poem in epic verse, framed as a revelation from a goddess
A mathematical treatise on geometry
quiz.explanation: Parmenides wrote in the hexameter verse of Homer, framing his arguments as the teaching of a goddess. Riddling prose was Heraclitus’ style.

quiz.question: Why, according to Parmenides, can what-is not have come into being?
options: Because the gods forbade it
Because it could come neither from what-is-not, which does not exist, nor from what-is, which already exists
Because the senses show us that nothing ever changes
Because everything is made of water
quiz.explanation: His argument is purely logical: coming-to-be would require something to come from nothing, which is impossible, or from something that already is, which is not coming-to-be at all.

quiz.question: Parmenides held that when our senses conflict with reason, we should trust our senses.
quiz.explanation: The goddess tells the traveler not to follow the aimless eye and echoing ear but to judge by reason.

quiz.question: What is the method of reductio ad absurdum, as used by Zeno?
options: Collecting many observations until a general law appears
Appealing to the authority of a respected teacher
Reducing a complex theory to its simplest elements
Assuming an opponent’s view and showing that it leads to absurd consequences
quiz.explanation: Zeno assumed that there is motion and plurality, then derived absurdities from those assumptions to defend Parmenides indirectly.

quiz.question: Which of Zeno’s paradoxes argues that a moving object is at rest at every instant?
options: The Arrow
The Dichotomy
Achilles and the Tortoise
The Moving Rows
quiz.explanation: The Arrow argues that at each instant the arrow occupies a space equal to itself and so is not moving, and since time is made of instants, it never moves.

quiz.question: How does the modern mathematical idea of a convergent series respond to the Dichotomy?
options: It proves that space is made of indivisible atoms
It shows that infinitely many ever-smaller distances can add up to a finite total, crossed in a finite time
It shows that Zeno miscounted the number of halves
It proves that motion is an illusion, as Parmenides claimed
quiz.explanation: One half plus one quarter plus one eighth and so on sums to exactly 1, so an infinite number of steps need not mean an infinite distance or time.

quiz.question: Melissus argued that motion is impossible because it would require empty space, which would be what-is-not.
quiz.explanation: Melissus, another follower of Parmenides, made this argument. The atomists on Day 7 respond by accepting that the void exists.

quiz.question: Which modern idea most closely resembles Parmenides’ view that coming-to-be and passing away are not ultimately real?
options: Evolution by natural selection
The block universe, in which past, present and future all equally exist
The idea that the economy is constantly growing
The theory that the universe is expanding
quiz.explanation: In the block universe nothing truly comes into being; all times simply exist. The comparison is imperfect, since the block has internal structure and Parmenides’ Being does not.

quiz.question: Aristotle responded to Zeno by distinguishing between a potential infinity and an actual infinity.
quiz.explanation: He argued that a distance is potentially divisible without end but is not actually made of infinitely many separate parts that must be crossed one by one.

quiz.question: What was the most important long-term effect of Parmenides and Zeno on Greek philosophy?
options: They ended interest in the natural world entirely
They convinced everyone that motion is an illusion
They forced later thinkers to explain how change is possible without anything coming from nothing
They proved that the senses are always reliable
quiz.explanation: The pluralists, the atomists and Plato all built their theories partly as answers to the Eleatic challenge, while still accepting that nothing comes from nothing.

goDeeper.body:
What exactly is Parmenides talking about when he says “it is”? The Greek verb *esti* can mean “exists,” but it can also be the “is” of predication (“the sky is blue”) or the “is” of truth (“it is so”). Scholars disagree about which sense drives the argument. G. E. L. Owen read Parmenides as arguing about whatever can be thought or spoken of. Charles Kahn argued for a “veridical” reading tied to truth and knowledge. Patricia Curd has proposed a “predicational” reading on which Parmenides is laying down requirements for what a genuine, fundamental entity must be like: each must be a single, unified nature, not a mixture of what it is and what it is not. On her reading, later pluralists like Empedocles and Anaxagoras were not rejecting Parmenides but accepting his standards and applying them to many entities instead of one.

A second debate concerns the relationship between the two parts of the poem. If the Way of Opinion is false, why did Parmenides develop it in such detail? Some read it as a dialectical exercise, others as a second-best account of appearances. The answer affects whether Parmenides was a strict monist at all.

On Zeno, the philosophical literature is rich. Adolf Grünbaum argued in the 20th century that the modern theory of the continuum, developed by Georg Cantor and others, fully resolves the paradoxes of extension. Others, following Thomson and later Paul Benacerraf, debated whether supertasks are logically possible. Mark Sainsbury’s *Paradoxes* is an accessible entry into these debates and a fine introduction to how philosophers analyze puzzling arguments generally.

readings.title: Paradoxes
readings.author: R. M. Sainsbury
readings.note: Chapter 1 analyzes Zeno’s paradoxes clearly and carefully; a model of how to take an absurd-seeming argument seriously.

readings.author: Jonathan Barnes
readings.note: A rigorous, argument-focused study; the chapters on Parmenides and Zeno reconstruct their reasoning step by step.

readings.title: Parmenides
readings.author: Plato
readings.note: The opening pages stage the meeting of Parmenides, Zeno and the young Socrates and describe the purpose of Zeno’s book.

readings.title: Physics, Book VI
readings.author: Aristotle
readings.note: Chapter 9 is our main source for the four paradoxes of motion and Aristotle’s replies; demanding but short.

questions: Is it really impossible to think about nothing? What are we doing when we say “there are no unicorns”?
Does a mathematical solution to Zeno’s paradoxes explain how motion is possible, or only describe it?
If reason and the senses truly conflicted on some question, which would you trust, and on what grounds?
